title: Dec 2015 (Paper II)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (50/50 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Locke
items.stem:
Who, among the following, advanced the theory that the mind is a tabula rasa at birth, and
acquires all ideas by experience ?
items.explanation: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), English empiricist philosopher John Locke advanced the foundational theory that the human mind at birth is a blank slate or 'tabula rasa', acquiring all ideas and knowledge through sensory experience and reflection.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Walter Pater
items.stem: Which of the following authors wrote Studies in the History of the Renaissance ?
items.explanation: Victorian aesthetic critic Walter Pater published Studies in the History of the Renaissance in 1873, containing his celebrated artistic essays on Leonardo da Vinci, Botticelli, and the famous 'Conclusion' advocating living with a hard, gem-like flame.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Jane Austen
items.stem: Whom does Harriet Smith finally marry in one of Jane Austen’s novels ?
items.explanation: In Jane Austen's Emma (1815), after Emma Woodhouse's well-intentioned but disastrous attempts to match Harriet Smith with the pompous vicar Mr. Elton and then Frank Churchill, Harriet finally accepts and marries the respectable young tenant farmer Robert Martin.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
A poet once referred to an old man as “A tattered coat upon a stick”.  That is an example of
__________.
items.explanation: In 'Sailing to Byzantium' (1928), W. B. Yeats writes: 'An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick', which is a direct metaphorical comparison equating the withered mortal body to a ragged coat hanging on a scarecrow's stick.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Alfred Lord Tennyson
items.stem: Which of these is NOT a pastoral elegy ?
items.explanation: Alfred Lord Tennyson's In Memoriam A. H. H. (1850) is a philosophical and devotional elegiac cycle, whereas Milton's Lycidas (1637), Arnold's Thyrsis (1865), and Shelley's Adonais (1821) are classical pastoral elegies using shepherds and classical pastoral imagery.

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
In Beckett’s Waiting for Godot the characters often use dislocated, repetitious and cliched
speech primarily to :
options: illustrate the essentially illogical, purposeless nature of the human condition
re-create the workings of the subconscious
mock the exaggerated dignity and wisdom of modern, self-professed intellectuals
reinforce the comic action of farcical plots
items.explanation: In Samuel Beckett's Theatre of the Absurd masterpiece Waiting for Godot (1953), Vladimir, Estragon, and Lucky use disjointed, repetitive, and circular dialogue to dramatize the existential futility, lack of meaning, and purposelessness of human life.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · George Puttenham, Philip Sidney, Walter Raleigh, Thomas Wyatt
items.stem: Which of the following sixteenth-century poets was NOT a courtier ?
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney, Sir Walter Raleigh, and Sir Thomas Wyatt were all prominent courtiers, diplomats, and statesmen in the Tudor court, whereas George Puttenham (author of The Arte of English Poesie, 1589) was a literary scholar and theorist rather than an active courtier.

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Patrick White
items.stem:
Patrick White published two novels in the 1950s iving the eras of pioneering and exploration
in Australian history an epic, ironic and psychological dimension.  The novels are :
(a)
A Fringe of Leaves
(b)
The Tree of Man
(c)
Voss
(d)
The Aunt’s Story
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Australian Nobel laureate Patrick White published two monumental novels in the 1950s chronicling Australian pioneering settlement and expedition: The Tree of Man (1955, depicting rural bush settlers Stan and Amy Parker) and Voss (1957, based on Ludwig Leichhardt's desert exploration).

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Mikhail Bakhtin
items.stem:
In ,which ,of ,the ,following ,works ,did ,Bakhtin ,propose ,his ,widely ,cited ,concept ,of ,the
‘Carnivalesque’ ?
options: “Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel”
items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin introduced his seminal conceptual framework of the 'chronotope' (literally 'time-space', the intrinsic interconnectedness of temporal and spatial relationships in literature) in his 1937–38 essay 'Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel'.

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Sebastian Faulks, Peter Ackroyd, Ian McEwan, Graham Swift
items.stem:
Match the columns :
(Author)
(Text)
(a)
Sebastian Faulks
(i)
Amsterdam
(b)
Peter Ackroyd
(ii)
Changing Places
(c)
Ian McEwan
(iii)
Hawksmoor
(d)
David Lodge
(iv)
Birdsong
Codes :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Sebastian Faulks wrote the WWI novel Birdsong (1993), Peter Ackroyd authored the visionary novel English Music (1992), Ian McEwan won the Booker Prize for Amsterdam (1998), and Graham Swift won the Booker Prize for Last Orders (1996).

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Allen Tate
items.stem: In New Criticism, the key term ‘tension’ is associated with :
items.explanation: In his influential essay 'Tension in Poetry' (1938), American New Critic Allen Tate defined 'tension' as the central criterion of poetic excellence, derived by synthesising the semantic extremes of 'extension' (literal denotation) and 'intension' (figurative connotation).

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Samuel Richardson
items.stem:
While compiling what sort of book did Samuel Richardson conceive of the idea for his Pamela
or Virtue Rewarded ?
options: an account of the plague in London
items.explanation: Samuel Richardson conceived the idea for his groundbreaking epistolary novel Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded (1740) while compiling Familiar Letters on Important Occasions, a practical conduct guide of model letters for country readers and servants.

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Siegfried Sassoon
items.stem:
Who among the war Poets ained notoriety in 1917, when disenchanted with the way the
war was being conducted he drafted his letter of “wilful defiance of the military authority”
which captured attention in the House of Commons, and was forcibly admitted to the war
hospital at Craiglockhart, primarily to avoid his being court-martialled ?
items.explanation: In July 1917, decorated British war poet Siegfried Sassoon caused widespread national sensation by issuing his defiant public anti-war declaration 'Finished with the War: A Soldier's Declaration', read aloud in the House of Commons, protesting against the prolonged slaughter.

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
If you cannot understand an argument and remark, “It’s Greek to me”,  you are quoting
__________.
items.explanation: The popular idiom 'It's Greek to me' originates in William Shakespeare's tragedy Julius Caesar (Act I, Scene 2), where Casca sarcastically reports Cicero's speech to Cassius: 'those that understood him smiled at one another and shook their heads; but, for mine own part, it was Greek to me.'

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Sir Walter Scott
items.stem: Which of the following works did Walter Scott compile ?
options: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
items.explanation: Sir Walter Scott compiled and published Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802–1803), a landmark three-volume collection of historical and romantic Scottish ballads gathered from oral traditions of the Scottish Borders.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Wole Soyinka, Chinua Achebe
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT written by Wole Soyinka ?
items.explanation: Home and Exile (2000) is a famous autobiographical essay collection written by Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe, whereas Kongi's Harvest (1965), The Interpreters (1965), and The Swamp Dwellers (1958) are all major works by Wole Soyinka.

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
In the Defense of Poesy Sidney says : “ Now as in eometry the oblique must be known as well
as right and in arithmetic, the odd as well as the even, so in the actions of our life who seeth
not the filthiness of evil wanteth a reat foil to perceive the beauty of virtue”.  Which of the
following forms of poesy offers a foil that helps us perceive the beauty of virtue ?
items.explanation: In The Defense of Poesy (1595), Sir Philip Sidney defends Comedy by comparing it to geometry, asserting that 'the oblique must be known as well as the right', meaning that viewing ridiculous human folly and errors teaches us by contrast to recognize and pursue virtuous conduct.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden, Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
John Dryden described a major English poet as “a rough diamond, and must first be polished
ere he shines .....” Identify him :
items.explanation: In his celebrated 'Preface to Fables Ancient and Modern' (1700), John Dryden affectionately praised Geoffrey Chaucer as 'a rough diamond, and must first be polished, e'er he shines', acknowledging Chaucer's vast genius while noting the primitive state of Middle English metre.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem:
In a remarkably proleptic insight, a critic wrote the following, anticipating Benedict Anderson’s
definition of the nation as “an imagined political community” :
“Most novels are in some sense knowable communities.  It is part of a traditional method –
an ,underlying ,stance ,and ,approach ,– ,that ,a ,novelist ,offers ,to ,show ,people ,and ,their
relationships in essentially knowable and communicable ways”.
Name the critic and the reference :
options: Van Wyck Brooks, The writer in America
Raymond Williams, The country and the city
Joseph Wood Krutch, The Modern Temper
T.S. Eliot, Notes Towards a Definition of culture
items.explanation: In The Country and the City (1973), Raymond Williams examined how communities and national affinities are imaginatively constructed and perceived across historical transformations of rural and urban spaces, anticipating Benedict Anderson's concept of 'imagined communities'.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Daniel
items.stem:
“Fair is my love, and cruel as she’s fair; Her brow-shades frown, although her eyes are sunny”.
The above lines are characterized by :
items.explanation: The line 'Fair is my love, and cruel as she's fair' (from Samuel Daniel's sonnet sequence Delia, 1592) employs antithesis, placing contrasting qualities (fairness and cruelty) in direct rhetorical opposition within the same poetic line.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope, Horace
items.stem:
In his “Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot” Pope tells us that as a poet he had benefited from “This
saving counsel, ‘keep your piece nine years’” – which enjoins on writer’s patience and reat
care before they rush to print.  Whose “counsel” is Pope referring to ?
items.explanation: In his verse epistle 'An Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot' (1735), Alexander Pope alludes to Horace's advice in Ars Poetica to withhold a manuscript for nine years ('nonumque prematur in annum') before publishing.

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit I: Drama · Inigo Jones, Ben Jonson
items.stem:
An English architect and stage-designer – Beginning 1605, joined Jacobean court to design
masques ,– ,contributed ,significantly ,to ,the ,spectacular ,theatre ,which ,succeeded ,the
commonwealth after his death – the first designer to use revolving screens to indicate scene-
changes on the English stage.
Identify this artist/designer.
items.explanation: Inigo Jones was the pioneering Jacobean court architect and theatrical designer who collaborated with Ben Jonson beginning in 1605 on elaborate royal court masques (introducing movable scenery, proscenium arches, and perspective stages to the English theater).

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
__________ may be defined as any departure from the rules of pronunciation or diction, for
the sake of rhyme or metre, or an unjustifiable departure from fact.
items.explanation: Poetic license denotes the freedom claimed by poets to depart from the conventional rules of grammar, syntax, diction, or pronunciation to achieve metrical regularity, rhythm, or specific aesthetic effects.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · C. P. Snow
items.stem: That Humanities and the sciences were in fact “two cultures” was suggested by __________.
options: Aldous Huxley in his oxford lectures on poetry
W.H. Anden in his oxford lectures on poetry
F.R. Leavis in his book, The Great Tradition
C.P. Snow in his Rede lecture
items.explanation: British novelist and physical chemist C. P. Snow delivered the Rede Lecture at Cambridge in May 1959, titled 'The Two Cultures and the Scientific Revolution', arguing that intellectual life in Western society was split into two hostile camps: sciences and humanities.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Chaueer satirizes the Monk because the Monk :
options: is too concerned with courtesy and matters of etiquette
cheats the poor peasants by selling them false religious relics
courts favour of wealthy people but spends no time with poor people
spends too much time hunting and too little time on religious duty
items.explanation: In 'The General Prologue' to The Canterbury Tales, Geoffrey Chaucer satirizes the Monk because, instead of cloistered prayer, study, and ascetic monastic vows, he indulges in hunting, rides fine horses, wears fur-lined sleeves, and loves a fat swan roast.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · James Baldwin
items.stem:
Divided into three sections this round-breaking work published in 1953 uses as the frame of
the spiritual and moral awakening of a fourteen-year-old during a Saturday night service in
a Harlem church.  Identify the work.
options: Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Are Watching God
James Baldwin’s Go Tell it on the Mountain
items.explanation: James Baldwin's semi-autobiographical debut novel Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953) is structured in three parts framed around a Sunday church service at the Temple of the Fire Baptized in Harlem, tracing the spiritual and racial awakening of John Grimes.

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Chartism, a political movement that took its name from the People’s Charter had six points.
Identify the one point on the following list that was NOT Chartist :
(a)
universal manhood sufferage
(b)
equal electoral districts
(c)
comprehensive insurance scheme for labour
(d)
vote by secret ballot
(e)
payment of MPs
(f)
no property qualifications for MPs
()
Annual parliaments
Codes :
items.explanation: The six demands of the 1838 People's Charter were: universal manhood suffrage, secret ballot, equal electoral districts, payment of MPs, abolition of property qualifications for MPs, and annual parliaments. A 'comprehensive insurance scheme for labour' was not among the six demands.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:
These beauteous forms,
Through a long absence, have been to me
As is a landscape to a blind man’s eye...
(“Tintern Abbey Lines”)
Which of the following rhetorical terms best suits these lines ?
items.explanation: In 'Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey' (1798), William Wordsworth uses litotes (ironic understatement through double negative) in asserting that the Wye valley forms 'have not been to me / As is a landscape to a blind man's eye'.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Mary Shelley
items.stem: The ‘monster’ in Frankenstein is NOT responsible for the death of :
items.explanation: In Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), the creature directly strangles William Frankenstein, Henry Clerval, and Elizabeth Lavenza, and frames Justine Moritz; Victor's father Alphonse Frankenstein dies peacefully in Victor's arms from apoplexy and grief.

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Which ,of ,the ,following ,plays ,of ,William ,Shakespeare ,is ONOT ,directly ,referred ,to ,in
T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land ?
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) directly quotes or alludes to The Tempest ('Those are pearls that were his eyes'), Hamlet (Ophelia's farewell: 'Good night, ladies'), and Coriolanus ('a broken Coriolanus'), but makes no direct citation from King Lear.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean & Caroline · Unit II: Poetry · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Identify the roup below which is known as the “Sons of Ben”.
options: Noel Coward, E.G. Craig, William Macready, Matheson, Lang
John Dryden, the Earl of Rochester, Samuel Butler
William Cartwright, Richard Corbett, Thomas Randolph
William Holman Hunt, John E. Millais, D.G. Rossetti, William Morris
items.explanation: The 'Sons of Ben' (or the 'Tribe of Ben') were early seventeenth-century Cavalier lyricists and dramatists who gathered around Ben Jonson at London taverns, including William Cartwright, Richard Corbett, Thomas Randolph, and Robert Herrick.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
Christopher Marlowe was one of the first major writers to affirm what can be identified as a
clearly homosexual sensibility.  Which drama of his deals with it ?
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's historical tragedy Edward II (c. 1592) is recognized as one of the earliest English plays to openly explore homosexual desire and aristocratic homoerotic passion through King Edward's devotion to Piers Gaveston.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem:
“When true silence falls we are still left with echo but are nearer nakedness.  One way of
looking at speech is to say that it is a constant stratagem to cover nakedness”.
Identify the playwright who underlines the significance of silence thus.
items.explanation: Harold Pinter, famous for his iconic 'Pinter pause' and pregnant theatrical silences, wrote perceptively in his 1962 speech 'Writing for the Theatre' on how language and pauses mask nakedness and psychological tension.

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
The determining feature of syllabic verse is neither __________ nor __________ but the number
of syllables in a line.
items.explanation: Unlike accentual verse (which measures stresses) or quantitative verse (which measures syllable duration/quantity), syllabic verse relies strictly on counting the total number of syllables per poetic line regardless of stress or quantity.

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem:
In Robert Browning’s dramatic monologue, which painter does Andrea del Sarto compare
himself to ?  What does he find lacking in his own work in comparison ?
items.explanation: In Robert Browning's dramatic monologue 'Andrea del Sarto' (1855), the 'Faultless Painter' wistfully acknowledges that although his technical draftsmanship exceeds Raphael's, Raphael possesses the burning 'soul' and visionary passion that Andrea lacks.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Southey
items.stem:
In which of the following does Robert Southey detail the Indian superstitions as an idolatry
to be suppressed by a civilizing protestant form of colonialism ?
items.explanation: Robert Southey's long narrative epic poem The Curse of Kehama (1810) draws heavily on Hindu mythology, presenting Hindu religious rituals and deities through an Orientalist lens depicting superstitious idolatry.

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Charlotte Perkins Gilman
items.stem:
The following is the classic ending of a celebrated novella in English :
“I kept on creeping just the same, but I looked at him over my shoulder.  ‘I’ve ot out at last’,
said I, “in spite of you and Jane.  And I’ve pulled off most of the papers, so you can’t put me
back !”
Now why should that man have fainted ?  But he did, and right across my path by the
wall, so that I had to creep over him every time !”
options: Johny Panic and the Bible of Dreams (Sylvia Plalth)
Where Are You Going, Where Have You Been ?  (Joyce C. Oates)
items.explanation: The closing line 'I've got out at last... and I've pulled off most of the paper, so you can't put me back!' as the narrator creeps obsessively over her husband's body is the climactic ending of Charlotte Perkins Gilman's feminist classic The Yellow Wallpaper (1892).

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Harriet Beecher Stowe
items.stem:
Harriet B. Stowe had wanted to write a work based on the life of an Afro-American writer
which was later published as :
options: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
items.explanation: Harriet Beecher Stowe's anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) drew inspiration from Josiah Henson's slave autobiography and other published narratives of formerly enslaved African Americans, galvanizing the abolitionist movement.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Samuel Johnson
items.stem: Samuel Johnson’s “Dissertation upon Poetry” is part of which of his following works ?
options: the final section of his preface to Shakespeare
a chapter of his novel Rasselas
the epilogue of his Lives of Poets
items.explanation: Dr. Samuel Johnson's renowned 'Dissertation upon Poetry' appears in Chapter X of his philosophical apologue The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759), delivered by the poet-philosopher Imlac.

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Terence Hawkes
items.stem:
A new series called “New Accents” was launched by Methuen in 1977.  The first title to be
published in the series was :
options: Making and Difference : Feminist Literary criticism
items.explanation: General editor Terence Hawkes launched Methuen's landmark 'New Accents' critical monograph series in 1977 with his own seminal introductory volume, Structuralism and Semiotics.

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:
“Humble and rustic life was enerally chosen, because, in that condition, the essential passions
of the heart find a better soil in which they can attain their maturity, are less under restraint,
and speak a plainer and more emphatic language... The language, too, of these men has been
adopted... because such men hourly communicate with the best objects from which the best
part of language is originally derived”.  Which of the following roups of the author’s poems
in the Lyrical Ballads (1800) contradict this statement in the “Preface to the Lyrical Ballads”,
as pointed out by S.T. Coleridge ?
options: “Ode on the Intimations of Immortality”, Prelude.
“Elegy Written in a country churchyard”, “Ode on the Popular Superstitions of the Highlands”.
items.explanation: In his 1800/1802 'Preface to Lyrical Ballads', William Wordsworth explains that 'humble and rustic life was generally chosen' because essential passions speak a plainer language, exemplifying this principle in narrative pastoral poems such as 'Michael', 'Ruth', and 'The Brothers'.

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · E. M. Forster
items.stem:
A remarkable novelist of the English Modernist phase who wrote a short book on what the
novel is (and why it matters) remarked, “Oh dear, yes - the novel tells a story”.  Identify the
novelist :
items.explanation: Modernist novelist E. M. Forster delivered the Clark Lectures at Cambridge in 1927, published as Aspects of the Novel, introducing classic critical distinctions between story and plot, and between flat and round characters.

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem:
What is the name of the angel, who, of those who owed allegeance to Satan, dared to protest
against his impious doctrine and left his company to return to God (Paradise Lost, Book V) ?
items.explanation: In Milton's Paradise Lost (Book V), the faithful seraph Abdiel stands alone among Satan's rebellious legions to denounce Satan's apostasy, declaring unyielding loyalty to God and defying the Luciferian revolt.

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Which ,of ,the ,following ,is ONOT ,a ,school ,associated ,with ,Romantic ,period ,in ,English
literature ?
items.explanation: The Fireside Poets (including Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, William Cullen Bryant, John Greenleaf Whittier, and Oliver Wendell Holmes) were 19th-century American domestic poets, whereas the Lake School, Cockney School, and Satanic School were English Romantic groupings.

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem: The idea of “new ethnicities” in post-war Britain was advanced by __________.
items.explanation: Cultural studies theorist Stuart Hall advanced the seminal concept of 'New Ethnicities' in his 1988 essay, arguing against essentialist notions of black identity and recognizing ethnic identities as historically constructed, diverse, and fluid.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse begins in a piece of dialogue :
“Yes, of course, if it’s fine tomorrow”, said Mrs. Ramsay. “But you’ll have to be up with
lark”, she added.
Present among the listeners of her remark is __________.
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse (1927) opens with Mrs Ramsay reassuring her young son James: 'Yes, of course, if it's fine tomorrow', granting him hope of their eagerly anticipated sailing expedition to the lighthouse.

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare, Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:
Match the phrase with character :
(a)
“motiveless malignity”
(i)
Macbeth
(b)
“Reason in Madness”
(ii)
Hamlet
(c)
“Supp’d full of horrors”
(iii)
Lear
(d)
“To be, or not to be”
(iv)
Iago
Codes :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge famously diagnosed Iago's evil as 'the motive-hunting of motiveless malignity'; Edgar observes 'Reason in madness' in the ruined King Lear; Macbeth admits he has no spur save 'Vaulting ambition'; and Othello is repeatedly addressed as the 'noble Moor'.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Laurence Sterne
items.stem: In Tristram Shandy the narrator’s presentation of his life and opinions is __________.
items.explanation: In Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (1759–67), the narration is notoriously digressive and progressive, frequently breaking linear chronology with philosophical tangents, blank pages, and lengthy family anecdotes.

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem:
The famous sonnet of John Milton beginning “When I consider how my light is spent...” ends
with ,__________.
options: Before me stares a wolfish eye, Behind me creeps a roan or sigh
They also serve who only stand and wait
And - which is more - you’ll be a Man, my son !
And bless him for the sake of him that’s one
items.explanation: Milton's Sonnet 19 ('When I consider how my light is spent') concludes with the consolation spoken by Patience: 'God doth not need / Either man's work or his own gifts... They also serve who only stand and wait.'

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2015 (Paper II)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction, short story · E. M. Forster
items.stem:
Her vision was of several caves.  She saw herself in one, and she was also outside it, watching
its entrance, for Aziz to pass in.  She failed to locate him.  It was the doubt that had often
visited her, but solid and attractive, like the hills.  “I am not –” speech was more difficult than
vision.  “I am not quite sure”.
The above extract from A Passage to India is about Adela’s cave experience.  Who is
questioning Adela ?
items.explanation: In Chapter 24 of E. M. Forster's A Passage to India (1924), during the courtroom trial following the Marabar Caves incident, the British District Superintendent of Police, Mr. McBryde, prosecutes the case and questions Adela Quested.
